title: Struct assignment copies the value
options: Compile error: cannot assign a struct to another variable
explanation: Structs are value types, so `var b = a` copies the whole value; mutating b.X changes only the copy and a.X stays 1. It would print 2 only if P were a class (reference type), and assigning structs is perfectly legal.

title: Record equality vs reference equality
options: True False
False False
True True
False True
explanation: Records are reference types with compiler-generated value-based equality: == compares the declared members, so two Persons named Ann are equal. They are still two separate heap objects, so ReferenceEquals returns false.

title: Primary constructor parameters in classes
options: The compiler generates a public init-only property Name, exactly as for a positional record
It is implicitly readonly, so assigning `name = "x"` inside a method is a compile error
It is only visible in field initializers, so using it inside a method like Hi() is a compile error
It is in scope in the whole class body; since Hi() uses it, it is captured in a hidden field
explanation: Unlike positional records, class primary constructor parameters do not become public properties. They are parameters in scope throughout the type; when a member references one, the compiler stores it in an unnamed field. They are also mutable, which is why many teams copy them into explicit readonly fields.

title: Method hiding with new vs override
options: B
A
AB
Compile error: Name must be marked override
explanation: `new` hides the base method instead of overriding it, so the virtual slot still points to A.Name. Calling through a variable of static type A therefore runs A's implementation. Only `override` would make the call dispatch to B; `new` compiles fine (it just suppresses the hiding warning).

title: Calling a default interface method
options: Prints "hi" because G inherits the default implementation as a public method
Compile error: G has no member Hello; you must call it through an IGreeter reference
Runtime MissingMethodException because G does not implement Hello
Compile error: classes must explicitly implement every interface member
explanation: Default interface members are not inherited into the class's public surface; they are only reachable through the interface type, e.g. `((IGreeter)g).Hello()` or `IGreeter g = new G();`. The class is not required to implement the member, so it compiles until you call Hello on the concrete type.

title: Virtual call from a base constructor
options: init|ctor
NullReferenceException is thrown
init|
explanation: In C#, derived field initializers run before the base constructor, but the derived constructor body runs after it. The base constructor's virtual call dispatches to Derived.Print, where _s is already "init" but _t is still null (interpolated as empty). This is why calling virtual members from constructors is discouraged.

title: Generic covariance rules
question: Which assignment compiles?
options: IEnumerable<object> xs = new List<string>();
List<object> xs = new List<string>();
IList<object> xs = new List<string>();
IEnumerable<object> xs = new List<int>();
explanation: IEnumerable<out T> is covariant, so a sequence of strings can be used as a sequence of objects. List<T> and IList<T> are invariant because they accept writes (adding an int to a List<string> would be unsafe). Variance also only applies to reference type arguments, so List<int> cannot convert to IEnumerable<object>.

title: Static fields in generic types
explanation: Each closed constructed type (Counter<int>, Counter<string>) is a distinct type with its own static fields. Counter<int>.Count is incremented twice and Counter<string>.Count once. This is often used deliberately, e.g. per-type caches, but surprises people who expect one shared static.

title: Lambda capture in a for loop
explanation: Lambdas capture variables, not values. A for loop declares a single variable i shared by all iterations, so every lambda sees its final value 3. (Since C# 5, foreach creates a fresh variable per iteration, so the same code with foreach prints the expected values.) Copying to a local inside the loop fixes it.

title: What the event keyword restricts
question: A class declares `public event EventHandler? Changed;`. What can code OUTSIDE that class do with Changed?
options: Only subscribe and unsubscribe with += and -=
Subscribe, unsubscribe and raise it with Changed?.Invoke(...)
Replace all handlers by assigning Changed = handler
Read the invocation list and invoke handlers one by one
explanation: The event keyword wraps a delegate field so external code gets only add/remove accessors. Raising the event or assigning/clearing the whole delegate is only allowed inside the declaring type, which is the main difference from a public delegate field.

title: Event subscriptions keeping objects alive
question: Short-lived view models subscribe to a singleton's event in their constructor (`clock.Tick += OnTick;`) and never unsubscribe. Memory grows over time. Why?
options: Event handlers are pinned by the GC, which blocks compaction and keeps the heap growing
Each += allocates a dedicated thread that only exits when the publisher is disposed
The view models are collected, but their handlers stay in the finalization queue forever
The singleton's delegate list references every view model, so they stay reachable
explanation: A delegate stores a reference to its target object. While the long-lived publisher keeps the handler in its invocation list, every subscriber is reachable from a GC root and can never be collected. Unsubscribe (e.g. in Dispose) or use a weak-event approach when publisher outlives subscribers.

title: Deferred execution of Where
options: InvalidOperationException: collection was modified
explanation: Where returns a lazily evaluated query; nothing runs until it is enumerated. Count() enumerates the list as it is at that moment, [1,2,3,4], so 2, 3 and 4 match. There is no modification exception because the Add happens before enumeration starts, not during it.

title: Multiple enumeration of a lazy query
explanation: q is a query, not a materialized collection, so each terminal operator re-runs the whole pipeline: Sum enumerates 3 elements and Max enumerates them again. With expensive projections, I/O or database queries this doubles the work; call ToList() once if you need the results multiple times.

title: Single with more than one match
question:
What happens when this runs?

var x = new[] { 1, 2, 2 }.Single(n => n == 2);
options: It returns 2, the first matching element
It returns 0, the default value of int, because the match is ambiguous
It returns 2 and logs a warning about duplicates
It throws InvalidOperationException: more than one element matches
explanation: Single asserts that exactly one element matches and throws if there are zero or several. First returns the first match, and SingleOrDefault returns default only when nothing matches (it still throws on multiple matches). Use Single when duplicates indicate a bug.

title: IEnumerable variable over an EF DbSet
options: Enumerable.Where is bound, so the whole table is loaded and filtered in memory
EF Core translates the filter to SQL because the runtime type is still a DbSet<Order>
It fails to compile because DbSet<Order> cannot be assigned to IEnumerable<Order>
EF Core throws because client evaluation is disabled for top-level filters
explanation: Extension method overloads are chosen by the static type. With IEnumerable<Order>, Where is LINQ-to-Objects taking a delegate, so EF just streams the whole table and the predicate runs in C#. Keep the variable typed as IQueryable<Order> so Queryable.Where receives an expression tree that EF translates to a SQL WHERE.

title: Rethrowing with throw vs throw ex
question: Inside `catch (Exception ex) { Log(ex); ... }`, why is `throw;` preferred over `throw ex;`?
options: `throw ex;` wraps the caught exception in an AggregateException, hiding its type
`throw;` is faster because it skips running the enclosing finally blocks
`throw;` keeps the original stack trace; `throw ex;` restarts it at the rethrow
`throw ex;` does not compile inside a catch block that declares a variable
explanation: A bare `throw;` rethrows the current exception unchanged, keeping the frames where it originated. `throw ex;` throws the same object as if it started here, so the original failure location is lost from the stack trace, which makes production debugging much harder. Neither form skips finally blocks or wraps the exception.

title: What nullable reference types do at runtime
question: A library with `<Nullable>enable</Nullable>` exposes `public int Len(string s) => s.Length;`. An older project without nullable annotations calls `Len(null)`. What happens?
options: The runtime throws ArgumentNullException before entering Len, due to the annotation
The call fails to compile in the calling project because Len's parameter is non-nullable
Nothing stops it; NRT is compile-time only, so s.Length throws NullReferenceException
Len receives an empty string because non-nullable parameters are coerced at runtime
explanation: Nullable reference types only change compiler warnings and metadata; there are no injected runtime checks. Callers that ignore or don't see the annotations can still pass null. Public APIs should still validate arguments, e.g. with ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull(s).

title: Return value when finally changes a local
options: Compile error: cannot assign in finally after return
explanation: The return expression is evaluated (and the int copied) before the finally block runs. Changing the local x afterwards does not affect the already-captured return value. (If x were a reference to a mutable object, mutations to that object would be visible.)

title: Collection expressions with spread
options: A jagged array: 1, [2, 3], 4
Compile error: the spread element only works with List<T>
An array that shares storage with b, so changing b[0] changes a
A new int[] containing 1, 2, 3, 4
explanation: C# 12 collection expressions build the target type from the listed elements, and `..b` spreads (copies) each element of b in place. The result is a fresh array with no link to b. Spreads work for any enumerable and targets such as arrays, List<T>, Span<T> and other collection types.

title: Mutating a dictionary key after insertion
question: A class Key overrides Equals/GetHashCode using its mutable Name property. You do `dict[k] = 1; k.Name = "changed";` and then call `dict.ContainsKey(k)`. What is the most likely result?
options: true, because the dictionary stores a reference to k and compares by reference first
false, because the lookup uses the new hash code and searches the wrong bucket
true, because Dictionary rehashes keys automatically when their properties change
An InvalidOperationException because the key was modified after it was inserted
explanation: Dictionary<TKey,TValue> computes the hash once at insertion. If the hash-relevant state changes, lookups compute a new hash, probe the wrong bucket and miss the entry, which is effectively lost. Keys must be immutable with respect to Equals/GetHashCode; records or readonly structs make good keys.

title: Why the GC uses generations
question: Why does the .NET garbage collector divide the managed heap into generations 0, 1 and 2?
options: Each generation belongs to a different thread, which avoids locking during allocation
Most objects die young, so frequent gen 0 collections reclaim most garbage cheaply
Generations separate value types from reference types so each can be collected differently
Objects in gen 2 are never collected, which avoids long pauses
explanation: The generational hypothesis says new objects are likely to become garbage quickly. Collecting gen 0 often is cheap because it is small; survivors are promoted, and gen 2 (long-lived objects) is collected rarely. Gen 2 is still collected, and generations have nothing to do with threads or value types.

title: GC.SuppressFinalize in Dispose
question: In the standard dispose pattern for a class with a finalizer, why does Dispose() call `GC.SuppressFinalize(this)`?
options: It forces an immediate garbage collection so the object's memory is reclaimed right away
It prevents other code from calling Dispose a second time on the same instance
It releases the object's unmanaged memory directly instead of waiting for the GC
Resources are already released, so finalization is unnecessary and can be skipped
explanation: Objects with finalizers survive at least one extra GC because they must be queued and finalized first. After deterministic cleanup in Dispose, suppressing finalization lets the GC reclaim the object normally. It does not trigger a collection or guard against double Dispose; Dispose must be idempotent on its own.

title: Large buffers per request
question: A service allocates `new byte[1_000_000]` for each request. Under load, profiling shows frequent gen 2 collections and a fragmented heap. What explains it and what is a good fix?
options: 85,000+ byte arrays go on the LOH, collected with gen 2 and not compacted by default; use ArrayPool<byte>
Arrays are value types, so each one is copied into gen 2 on allocation; switch to List<byte> instead
Large arrays are pinned automatically, which blocks gen 0 collections; call GC.Collect after each request
The JIT allocates large arrays on the stack and spills them to gen 2; mark the method with [SkipLocalsInit]
explanation: Objects at or above the 85,000-byte threshold are allocated on the LOH. LOH allocations count toward gen 2 budgets, so churning large buffers triggers expensive full collections, and since the LOH isn't compacted by default it fragments. Reusing buffers via ArrayPool<T> removes the churn.

title: DATAS in .NET 9 Server GC
question: After moving a containerized ASP.NET Core service from .NET 8 to .NET 9 with Server GC, its heap is noticeably smaller when idle and grows with load. Which GC feature, enabled by default in .NET 9, explains this?
options: Concurrent GC, which now runs every gen 2 collection on a background thread
GC conserve memory mode, which is now set to 9 by default for Server GC
DATAS, which adapts the number of heaps and the allocation budget to the app's long-lived data size
Regions, which return each 4 MB region to the OS after every gen 0 GC
explanation: Dynamic Adaptation To Application Sizes (opt-in in .NET 8, default in .NET 9 with Server GC) starts with one heap and grows or shrinks heap count and budgets based on load, so heap size tracks live data rather than core count. Classic Server GC sizes aggressively for throughput regardless of how much data the app keeps.

title: Sequential awaits vs Task.WhenAll
options: Both take about 1 s because await runs calls in parallel automatically
Both take about 3 s because WhenAll awaits the tasks one by one
A takes about 3 s and B about 1 s
A takes about 1 s and B about 3 s because WhenAll adds scheduling overhead
explanation: In A, each call starts only after the previous one completes, so the waits add up. In B all three tasks are started first and WhenAll completes when the last one finishes, so independent I/O overlaps. await itself never starts other work concurrently.

title: Blocking on async code in a UI app
question: A WinForms button handler runs `var text = LoadAsync().Result;`. LoadAsync does `return await httpClient.GetStringAsync(url);`. The window freezes forever. Why?
options: The UI thread blocks on .Result, yet the continuation must resume on that thread
HttpClient cannot be used from a UI thread, so the request silently never completes
.Result starts a nested message loop that never processes the HTTP response
LoadAsync runs synchronously, so GetStringAsync waits for the button handler to return
explanation: await captures the current SynchronizationContext and posts the continuation back to it. The UI thread is stuck inside .Result, so the continuation can never run and the task never completes. Fix by awaiting all the way up (async event handler), or use ConfigureAwait(false) in library code that doesn't need the context.

title: Exceptions from async void
options: "caught" is printed because the try block surrounds the call to Boom()
The exception is stored in the returned Task and silently ignored by the runtime
It fails to compile because async void methods are not allowed to throw exceptions
"caught" isn't printed; the exception crashes the process from the thread pool
explanation: Boom returns to the caller at its first await, so the try block has already exited when the exception occurs. An async void method has no Task to hold the exception, so it is rethrown on the captured context (here, the thread pool) as an unhandled exception. Use async Task except for event handlers.

title: ConfigureAwait(false) in ASP.NET Core
question: Which statement about ConfigureAwait(false) is accurate for modern .NET?
options: It makes the awaited operation itself run on a thread-pool thread instead of on the caller's thread
ASP.NET Core app code doesn't need it (no SynchronizationContext), but libraries should still use it
It is required in ASP.NET Core controllers to avoid the classic .Result/.Wait() sync-over-async deadlock
It makes HttpContext inaccessible after the await in ASP.NET Core, so it must be avoided in controllers
explanation: ConfigureAwait(false) only affects where the continuation runs: it tells await not to marshal back to the captured context. ASP.NET Core has no SynchronizationContext, so there is no context to deadlock on, and HttpContext stays usable. Libraries might be called from UI or legacy ASP.NET apps that do have a context, so they still benefit.

title: Awaiting a ValueTask twice
question: A method returns ValueTask<int> backed by a pooled IValueTaskSource. A caller stores it and awaits it twice. What is the consequence?
options: The second await returns the cached result, exactly like awaiting a Task<int> twice
Undefined behavior: the recycled source may yield another operation's result or throw
The second await re-executes the asynchronous operation and returns its fresh result value
The compiler rejects storing a ValueTask in a local variable to prevent reuse
explanation: ValueTask is designed to be consumed once. After the first await the underlying IValueTaskSource can be reset and reused by another operation, so a second await (or concurrent awaits, or .Result before completion) may observe someone else's result or throw. Call .AsTask() if you need to await multiple times.

title: Lost updates with ++ across threads
question: Two threads each run `counter++` one million times on a shared int field. The final value is often below 2,000,000. What is the simplest correct fix?
options: Mark the field as volatile
Make counter a static field
Replace int with long
Use Interlocked.Increment(ref counter)
explanation: counter++ is a read-modify-write of three steps, so two threads can read the same value and one increment is lost. Interlocked.Increment performs it atomically. volatile only affects visibility and reordering, not atomicity of the compound operation; static or long changes nothing about the race.

title: await inside a lock statement
options: Compile error: await is not allowed in a lock body; use SemaphoreSlim.WaitAsync
It compiles and holds the lock across the await on whichever thread resumes
It compiles, but the lock is released automatically at the await and reacquired after
It compiles only when _sync is a System.Threading.Lock instance
explanation: Monitor-based locks are thread-affine: the thread that enters must exit, but after an await the continuation may run on another thread. The compiler therefore forbids await in a lock body. SemaphoreSlim(1, 1) with WaitAsync/Release in a try/finally is the usual async-compatible mutual exclusion.

title: System.Threading.Lock with the lock statement
question: In C# 13 / .NET 9 you write `private readonly Lock _gate = new();` and `lock (_gate) { ... }`. What does the compiler do differently than for `lock (someObject)`?
options: It turns the block into an async lock that allows await inside the lock body
Nothing; the lock statement always uses Monitor.Enter/Exit on any object type
It calls _gate.EnterScope() and disposes the scope instead of Monitor.Enter/Exit
It acquires a reader lock so that multiple threads may enter the block simultaneously
explanation: When the lock target is statically a System.Threading.Lock, the compiler uses the type's dedicated API (EnterScope returning a ref struct scope) rather than the Monitor object-header mechanism. It is still an exclusive, synchronous lock, so await inside the block remains disallowed.

title: ConcurrentDictionary.GetOrAdd value factory
question: `cache.GetOrAdd(key, k => CreateExpensiveClient(k))` is called concurrently for the same new key. Logs show CreateExpensiveClient ran three times. Why, and how do you guarantee a single creation?
options: GetOrAdd is not thread-safe for new keys; wrap every call in a lock on the dictionary
The dictionary was resized, which re-runs pending factories; set a larger initial capacity
The factory runs outside the lock, so racing threads may each call it; store Lazy<T> values
The key's GetHashCode is not deterministic across threads; override it to return a stable constant
explanation: All ConcurrentDictionary operations are thread-safe, but GetOrAdd and AddOrUpdate are not atomic with respect to the user delegate, which is invoked outside the lock to avoid blocking. Only one result is stored, yet several may be created. Using ConcurrentDictionary<TKey, Lazy<TValue>> ensures the expensive work runs once.

title: When attribute constructors run
question: A custom attribute's constructor writes to a log. You apply `[Audit("orders")]` to a class. When does that constructor run?
options: On each reflection lookup such as GetCustomAttributes, which creates a new instance
Once, when the assembly is loaded, and the instance is cached for later lookups
Every time an instance of the decorated class is constructed, before its constructor
At compile time, with the resulting object serialized into the assembly metadata
explanation: Attribute arguments are stored as metadata at compile time, but the attribute object is not created until code asks for it via reflection. Each GetCustomAttribute(s) call instantiates new attribute objects and runs the constructor again, which is why expensive logic does not belong in attribute constructors.

title: Reflection in a trimmed Native AOT app
question: A plugin loader does `Activator.CreateInstance(Type.GetType(config["Handler"])!)`. It works with `dotnet run`, but the Native AOT published app fails because the type cannot be found. Why?
options: Native AOT apps cannot call Activator.CreateInstance under any circumstances
Type.GetType only searches the GAC, which doesn't exist in AOT-compiled apps
Configuration values are not available in AOT apps until after startup completes
The trimmer removed the type because only a config string refers to it
explanation: Trimming keeps only code it can prove is used. A type named in a config string is not statically referenced, so it is removed and reflection fails at runtime (the build emits trim warnings). Reference the types statically, annotate with DynamicallyAccessedMembers, or replace reflection with source generators.

title: Span<T> as a class field
options: Span<T> fields must be marked readonly when declared inside a class
Span<T> is a ref struct, so it can't be a field of a class; use Memory<byte>
Span<T> can only wrap stackalloc memory, never heap-allocated managed arrays like byte[]
Span<T> requires an unsafe context when it is used as an instance field
explanation: Span<T> may point into stack memory, so the compiler ensures it never escapes to the heap: it can't be a field of a class or regular struct, be boxed, or be captured by a lambda. Memory<T> is the heap-storable counterpart and exposes .Span when you need to process it synchronously.

title: ArrayPool.Rent semantics
question: What is guaranteed about `var buf = ArrayPool<byte>.Shared.Rent(1000);`?
options: buf.Length is exactly 1000 and the array is zeroed, just like new byte[1000]
buf.Length is at least 1000, and the array may hold data from a previous renter
buf is allocated on the stack with stackalloc and freed automatically at scope end
buf must not be returned to the pool if it is larger than the requested size
explanation: Pools hand out arrays in size buckets, so Rent may return a bigger array than requested and does not clear it. Track the length you actually need instead of using buf.Length, and call Return when done (optionally with clearArray: true for sensitive data). Never use the array after returning it.

title: Defensive copies with in parameters
options: It compiles and c._n ends up as 2, because in passes the struct by reference
Compile error: cannot call a non-readonly method on an in parameter
Runtime exception: attempted to modify the target of a readonly reference
It compiles; each call mutates a hidden defensive copy, so c stays unchanged
explanation: An in parameter is a readonly reference. Since Next is not a readonly member, the compiler cannot prove it won't mutate, so it silently copies the struct before calling it. The caller's value never changes, and large structs pay a copy per call. Marking the struct or member readonly removes the defensive copy.

title: Native AOT trade-offs
question: A team considers publishing a minimal API with Native AOT. Which is a real trade-off?
options: Faster startup and smaller footprint, but no JIT, so no runtime code generation
The app still needs the .NET runtime installed on the host, but it starts faster
Throughput is always higher because code is optimized using runtime profile data
Reflection is completely unavailable, including reading custom attributes on types
explanation: Native AOT compiles to a self-contained native executable ahead of time, which helps startup and footprint. Without a JIT, features like Reflection.Emit are unsupported, and trimming removes unreferenced code. Basic reflection still works on preserved types, and peak throughput can be lower because Dynamic PGO is unavailable.

title: Tiered compilation and Dynamic PGO
question: A hand-rolled benchmark shows the first few thousand calls of a method are much slower than later calls on .NET 8+. What runtime behavior explains it?
options: The GC runs in workstation mode until the app has allocated 1 GB, then switches to server mode
IL is interpreted until the method has been called 30 times, then it is compiled once
Methods start as quick unoptimized tier-0 code; hot ones are re-JITted at tier 1 with PGO
ReadyToRun code is always slower and is replaced with JIT code only after a full GC
explanation: Tiered compilation JITs quickly first, then recompiles methods that are called often (with on-stack replacement for long loops). Since .NET 8 Dynamic PGO is on by default, so tier-1 code uses observed types and branches for inlining and devirtualization. Benchmarks need warmup (as BenchmarkDotNet does) to measure steady state.

title: Meaning of a scoped lifetime
question: In an ASP.NET Core app, a service is registered with `AddScoped<ICart, Cart>()`. How many instances are created?
options: One for the whole lifetime of the application process
A new one every time it is injected anywhere
One per HTTP request, shared within that request
One per thread-pool thread handling requests
explanation: ASP.NET Core creates a DI scope per request, and scoped services are created once per scope. Singleton gives one instance for the app, and transient gives a new instance per resolution. Scopes are not related to threads, which matters because async code can hop threads.

title: Multiple registrations of one interface
options: INotifier resolves SmsNotifier; IEnumerable<INotifier> yields both, in registration order
INotifier resolves EmailNotifier; IEnumerable<INotifier> yields only EmailNotifier
Startup throws because INotifier is registered twice
INotifier resolves EmailNotifier; IEnumerable<INotifier> yields both
explanation: The default container resolves the last registration for a single service, while IEnumerable<T> returns every registration. Duplicate registrations don't throw; use TryAdd* if you want 'register only if missing' semantics, e.g. in library extension methods.

title: Singleton depending on a scoped DbContext
question: `PriceCache` is registered as a singleton and its constructor takes `AppDbContext` (registered by AddDbContext). What happens when the app runs in the Development environment?
options: It works; the container creates a fresh DbContext for each method call on PriceCache
The DbContext is silently promoted to singleton and nothing is reported in any environment
PriceCache is silently downgraded to scoped so it gets one DbContext per request
Scope validation throws: scoped AppDbContext can't be consumed from singleton PriceCache
explanation: This is a captive dependency: a long-lived service capturing a shorter-lived one. In Development, ASP.NET Core enables scope validation and detects it. Without validation, one DbContext would live for the whole app, used concurrently and growing its change tracker. Inject IServiceScopeFactory or make the consumer scoped.

title: Transient disposables from the root provider
question: A background loop calls `app.Services.GetRequiredService<ReportWriter>()` each iteration. ReportWriter is transient and implements IDisposable. Memory grows steadily. Why?
options: Transient services are never garbage collected because the container caches them
The root provider holds every disposable transient until it is disposed at shutdown
IDisposable objects are always placed on the Large Object Heap and rarely collected
GetRequiredService creates a new root provider, with its own caches, on each call
explanation: The service provider holds references to the IDisposable instances it creates so it can dispose them when the scope ends. Resolving from the root means the 'scope' is the app, so every instance is kept alive. Create a scope per iteration (IServiceScopeFactory.CreateScope) and resolve from it.

title: Configuration source precedence
question: Payment:TimeoutSeconds is set in appsettings.json, in appsettings.Production.json, and as environment variable `Payment__TimeoutSeconds`. With a default WebApplicationBuilder in Production, which value wins?
options: appsettings.json, because it is loaded first
The environment variable
appsettings.Production.json, because environment files always win
None; duplicate keys cause a startup exception
explanation: Configuration providers are layered and later sources override earlier ones: appsettings.json, then appsettings.{Environment}.json, user secrets (Development only), environment variables, then command-line arguments. The double underscore in environment variable names maps to the ':' hierarchy separator.

title: Reading reloaded options in a singleton
question: A singleton service must observe updated FeatureFlags values when appsettings.json changes on disk, without restarting. Which interface should it inject?
options: IOptions<FeatureFlags>
IOptionsSnapshot<FeatureFlags>
IConfigureOptions<FeatureFlags>
IOptionsMonitor<FeatureFlags>
explanation: IOptions<T> is computed once and never changes. IOptionsSnapshot<T> is recomputed per scope but is itself scoped, so it cannot be injected into a singleton. IOptionsMonitor<T> is a singleton exposing CurrentValue and OnChange notifications. IConfigureOptions<T> configures options rather than reading them.

title: String interpolation in log calls
question: A hot path runs `_logger.LogDebug($"Processed order {order.Id} in {elapsed} ms");` while the minimum level in production is Information. What are the problems?
options: It formats the string even with Debug off and loses OrderId/elapsed as structured data
None; the logger detects the disabled level and skips building the interpolated string
The call throws FormatException because the braces are interpreted as a message template
Only a performance problem; structured properties are inferred from the interpolation holes
explanation: Interpolation runs before LogDebug is called, so it allocates a string regardless of the log level, and the provider only sees a finished string. Use a message template such as LogDebug("Processed order {OrderId} in {Elapsed} ms", order.Id, elapsed), or the [LoggerMessage] source generator for zero-allocation, level-checked logging.

title: Middleware pipeline execution order
options: ACEBD
ABCDE
ACEDB
EDCBA
explanation: Middleware run in registration order on the way in and in reverse on the way out. A writes A, calls next; the second writes C, calls next; Run is terminal and writes E. Control then unwinds: D, then B. This nesting is why ordering matters for exception handling, auth and response modifications.

title: Exception handler placement
question: A custom middleware registered BEFORE `app.UseExceptionHandler("/error")` throws an exception. What happens?
options: UseExceptionHandler handles it, since it catches exceptions from the whole pipeline
The exception is swallowed by Kestrel and the request continues to the endpoint
It escapes UseExceptionHandler, which only catches exceptions from middleware after it
ASP.NET Core reorders the middleware so the exception handler always runs before others
explanation: Middleware wrap the ones registered after them. The exception handler can only catch exceptions that propagate up through its own call to next, so anything registered before it is outside its try/catch. That is why UseExceptionHandler (or the developer exception page) is registered first.

title: Route constraint mismatch
question: With `app.MapGet("/items/{id:int}", (int id) => ...);` and no other routes, what does `GET /items/abc` return?
options: 404 Not Found, because the route constraint does not match
400 Bad Request with a model binding error
200 OK with id set to 0
500 Internal Server Error from a FormatException
explanation: Route constraints participate in matching: 'abc' isn't an int, so the endpoint is not selected and no other endpoint matches, producing 404. Constraints are meant to disambiguate routes, not to validate input; for input validation you would accept the value and return 400 yourself.

title: Latency spike from sync-over-async
question: Under a traffic burst, an ASP.NET Core API's p99 latency jumps to several seconds while CPU stays around 20% and the thread count climbs slowly. Controllers call `_client.GetAsync(url).Result`. What is the most likely cause?
options: Kestrel's MaxConcurrentConnections limit was reached, so new sockets wait in the queue
The GC is running a blocking gen 2 collection on every request under load
HttpClient serializes all requests to the same host by default, one at a time
Thread-pool starvation: threads block on I/O while new ones are injected only slowly
explanation: Blocking on async I/O ties up a thread for the whole wait. When a burst blocks all pool threads, queued work (including continuations that would unblock them) waits while the pool slowly adds threads, so latency soars with low CPU. Make the call chain async end to end.

title: 401 vs 403
question: A user with a valid token calls an endpoint protected by `[Authorize(Roles = "Admin")]` but is not in the Admin role. What does ASP.NET Core return by default with JWT bearer authentication?
options: 401 Unauthorized
403 Forbidden
404 Not Found
400 Bad Request
explanation: 401 means the request isn't authenticated (challenge), while 403 means the user is authenticated but not permitted (forbid). Authorization failure for an authenticated user triggers the scheme's Forbid behavior, which for JWT bearer is a 403.

title: Authorizing by resource ownership
question: Only a document's author may edit it. The author ID is stored on the document in the database. What is the idiomatic ASP.NET Core approach?
options: Use [Authorize(Policy = "EditPolicy")] on the action and query the document inside the policy definition
Load the document, then call IAuthorizationService.AuthorizeAsync(User, document, "EditPolicy")
Create one role per document and check it on the action with [Authorize(Roles = ...)]
Put the document ID in a claim at login and compare it against the route in middleware
explanation: Attribute authorization runs before the action and has no access to the loaded resource. Resource-based authorization calls IAuthorizationService imperatively after loading the entity, passing it to an AuthorizationHandler<TRequirement, Document> that compares the author with the user's claims.

title: Revoked role still accepted
question: An admin's role was removed in the database, yet they keep calling admin endpoints successfully for another 50 minutes. The API uses JWT bearer authentication with 1-hour tokens. Why?
options: JWT bearer caches the user's database record for one hour by default to save lookups
Removing a role only takes effect after the app restarts and reloads its role cache
The authorization middleware skips role checks for tokens issued by the same server
Roles are claims in the signed token, validated locally until it expires
explanation: JWT validation checks signature, issuer, audience and lifetime locally; claims are trusted as issued. Changes to the source of truth aren't seen until a new token is obtained. Mitigate with short-lived access tokens plus refresh tokens, checking critical permissions server-side, or token revocation lists.

title: Unhandled exception in BackgroundService
question: Since .NET 6, what happens by default when ExecuteAsync of a BackgroundService throws an unhandled exception?
options: The exception is logged and the host stops
The exception is swallowed and the service silently stops while the app keeps running
The host restarts the BackgroundService automatically
The exception crashes the process without being logged
explanation: The default BackgroundServiceExceptionBehavior is StopHost, so the error is logged and the application shuts down, making failures visible (before .NET 6 the service just stopped silently). You can set it to Ignore, but usually you should catch and handle exceptions inside the loop.

title: Using a DbContext from a BackgroundService
question: A BackgroundService that processes an outbox every 10 seconds injects AppDbContext in its constructor. What is the correct fix?
options: Register AppDbContext as a singleton so that hosted services and controllers can share it
Register the BackgroundService with AddScoped instead of with AddHostedService
Inject IServiceScopeFactory and resolve AppDbContext from a new scope per iteration
Keep the injection but call ChangeTracker.Clear() at the end of every iteration
explanation: Hosted services are singletons, so injecting a scoped DbContext is a captive dependency (and fails scope validation in Development). Creating a scope per unit of work gives a fresh, short-lived context each time. A singleton DbContext isn't thread-safe and grows; hosted services can't be scoped.

title: Database checks in liveness probes
question: A Kubernetes liveness probe hits /healthz, which includes a SQL Server health check. A brief database failover causes every pod to be restarted. What is the better design?
options: Increase the liveness timeout so that the database check always has time to complete
Remove health checks entirely and rely on Kubernetes TCP socket probes for everything
Move the database check to a readiness endpoint; liveness checks only the process
Cache the database check result for an hour so the liveness probe never fails
explanation: Liveness answers 'should this container be restarted?', which a dependency outage doesn't fix. Readiness answers 'should traffic be routed here?'. MapHealthChecks with a HealthCheckOptions.Predicate on tags lets you expose separate endpoints so dependency failures take pods out of rotation without restart storms.

title: Saving a tracked entity
options: An UPDATE that sets only the Name column for blog 1
An UPDATE that sets every column of blog 1
Nothing, because Update(blog) was not called
A DELETE followed by an INSERT of the blog
explanation: Queried entities are tracked by default. The change tracker snapshots original values, detects that only Name changed and generates an UPDATE for that column. Calling Update() isn't needed for tracked entities; it would actually mark all properties as modified.

title: Modifying a no-tracking entity
options: The UPDATE is sent because SaveChanges compares all loaded entities
SaveChangesAsync throws because the entity was loaded without tracking
EF re-queries the blog and updates it, so n is 1
No UPDATE is sent and n is 0, because the context isn't tracking the entity
explanation: AsNoTracking skips change-tracker registration, which is faster for read-only queries, but the context then has no idea the object exists. To save changes you must attach it (e.g. db.Update(blog)) or query with tracking.

title: Parallel queries on one DbContext
question: In a controller, `await Task.WhenAll(db.Orders.CountAsync(), db.Customers.CountAsync());` intermittently fails. Why?
options: SQL Server does not allow two COUNT queries on one open connection
DbContext allows one operation at a time; starting a second one throws
Task.WhenAll cannot be used with tasks returned by EF Core queries
CountAsync returns a ValueTask, which Task.WhenAll cannot await together
explanation: A DbContext instance supports only one async operation at a time and detects concurrent use, throwing 'A second operation was started on this context instance'. Await the queries sequentially, or use separate contexts (e.g. IDbContextFactory) when real parallelism is needed.

title: Loading related entities
question: With a fresh DbContext and no lazy loading configured, `var blog = await db.Blogs.FirstAsync();` is followed by `blog.Posts.Count` (Posts is initialized to an empty List). Posts exist in the database. What is Count?
options: The real number of posts, because EF loads navigations on first access
0, because related data loads only via Include or explicit loading
It throws a LazyLoadingException on first access to Posts
The real number of posts, because collection navigations are always eager
explanation: EF Core doesn't load navigations automatically. You choose eager loading (Include), explicit loading (Entry(blog).Collection(b => b.Posts).LoadAsync()), or opt-in lazy loading via proxies. Without one of these the collection stays empty.

title: N+1 queries with lazy loading
question:
An endpoint with lazy-loading proxies enabled runs:

foreach (var user in await db.Users.ToListAsync())
    total += user.Orders.Count;

With 500 users, p95 latency is 4 s. What is the problem and fix?
options: The change tracker is too slow for 500 users; add AsNoTracking and keep the loop
ToListAsync buffers every user in memory; switch to AsAsyncEnumerable to stream them
Count on a navigation is evaluated on the client; add a database index on Orders.UserId
N+1 queries: each Orders access runs a query; project Select(u => u.Orders.Count())
explanation: Lazy loading issues a separate query the first time each user's Orders is touched: 1 query for users plus 500 for orders, each a round trip. Projecting the aggregate (or using Include when you need the entities) lets the database compute it in one query.

title: Projecting to a DTO
question: A list endpoint only needs Id and Name of products, which have 30 columns including a large Description. What does `db.Products.Select(p => new ProductDto(p.Id, p.Name)).ToListAsync()` achieve?
options: SQL selects only Id and Name, and the DTOs aren't tracked
SQL selects all columns, then EF maps two of them into the DTO
SQL selects only Id and Name, but each DTO is tracked by the change tracker
It fails because EF can't translate a constructor call
explanation: EF Core translates the projection into a SELECT of the referenced columns, avoiding transfer of unneeded data. Non-entity results aren't tracked, so there's no snapshot overhead either. Projection is one of the most effective EF read optimizations.

title: Cartesian explosion with multiple Includes
question: `db.Blogs.Include(b => b.Posts).Include(b => b.Contributors)` returns huge result sets and is slow for blogs with many posts and contributors. What is the cause and an EF Core remedy?
options: Include issues one query per blog; use AsNoTracking to batch them into one
EF loads Contributors lazily despite Include; call Load() explicitly instead
One JOIN query duplicates rows (posts x contributors); use AsSplitQuery()
Two Includes force client evaluation; add ToList() before the second Include
explanation: With single-query loading, two sibling collection Includes produce a cartesian product, so the row count multiplies. AsSplitQuery (or UseQuerySplittingBehavior globally) runs a query per collection, trading extra round trips and potential consistency issues for far less data duplication.

title: Bulk update with ExecuteUpdateAsync
question:
await db.Products
    .Where(p => p.CategoryId == 3)
    .ExecuteUpdateAsync(s => s.SetProperty(p => p.Price, p => p.Price * 1.1m));

Which statement is true?
options: It loads the matching products, updates them in memory, then waits for SaveChanges
It updates only the tracked entities in memory and sends nothing to the database
It sends one UPDATE at once without loading entities; tracked products keep stale prices
It sends one UPDATE per product, inside the transaction of the next SaveChanges call
explanation: ExecuteUpdate/ExecuteDelete translate directly to set-based SQL and execute right away, bypassing the change tracker. That is great for bulk operations, but tracked instances aren't refreshed and the statement isn't part of SaveChanges unless you use an explicit transaction.

title: Optimistic concurrency with a rowversion
question: An entity has `[Timestamp] public byte[] Version { get; set; }` on SQL Server. Two users load the same row, both edit and save. What happens on the second save?
options: DbUpdateConcurrencyException, since UPDATE ... WHERE Version = @original hits 0 rows
The second save silently overwrites the first one, so the last write wins
The second save blocks until the first user's transaction commits, then overwrites it
EF merges both users' changes column by column automatically and saves both
explanation: A concurrency token is added to the WHERE clause of UPDATE/DELETE. After the first save the database changes the rowversion, so the second statement matches no rows and EF throws. The app then decides how to resolve: reload and retry, merge, or show the conflict to the user.

title: Integration tests with WebApplicationFactory
question: What does `WebApplicationFactory<Program>` with `WithWebHostBuilder(b => b.ConfigureTestServices(s => ...))` provide?
options: It generates mocks for every registered service automatically and injects them into controllers
It deploys the app to a local Kestrel port and runs browser-based UI tests against it
It runs controllers directly, without the middleware pipeline, routing or filters
It hosts the real app in memory on a TestServer, with an HttpClient and swappable services
explanation: WebApplicationFactory uses the app's real startup (middleware, routing, DI) hosted on an in-memory TestServer, and CreateClient returns an HttpClient that bypasses the network. ConfigureTestServices runs after the app's registrations, so tests can swap e.g. external APIs or the database.

title: Pitfalls of the EF Core in-memory provider
question: Tests against the EF Core InMemory provider pass, but production on PostgreSQL fails on a query and a unique constraint. Why is this common?
options: The in-memory provider runs queries in parallel, which hides race conditions
It isn't relational: it skips many constraints, transactions and SQL translation
The in-memory provider uses a different C# compiler version than the app
Tests always run with lazy loading enabled, unlike the production configuration
explanation: The InMemory provider evaluates LINQ in memory and doesn't mimic relational behavior (raw SQL, transactions, constraint enforcement, case sensitivity). Microsoft recommends testing against the real database engine (e.g. in containers) or, at most, SQLite in-memory, and using repository fakes for pure unit tests.

title: Counting items per key
question: In .NET 9+, which call returns key/count pairs for words by first letter without materializing groups?
options: words.GroupBy(w => w[0]).Count()
words.CountBy(w => w[0])
words.ToLookup(w => w[0]).Count
words.Distinct(w => w[0])
explanation: CountBy (added in .NET 9) yields KeyValuePair<TKey,int> for each key directly. GroupBy(...).Count() returns the number of groups, not per-key counts, and ToLookup(...).Count is likewise the number of keys. Distinct has no key-selector overload (DistinctBy does).

title: Keyed services
question: Two IStorage implementations are registered with `AddKeyedSingleton<IStorage, BlobStorage>("blob")` and `AddKeyedSingleton<IStorage, DiskStorage>("disk")`. How does a constructor ask for the blob one?
options: Inject IStorage and the container picks by parameter name blob
Inject IEnumerable<IStorage> and filter by key at runtime
Inject Func<string, IStorage> and call it with "blob"
Annotate the parameter: [FromKeyedServices("blob")] IStorage storage
explanation: Keyed services (built into Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection since .NET 8) are resolved by key through [FromKeyedServices] or IServiceProvider.GetRequiredKeyedService. Keyed registrations are not returned for a plain IStorage parameter, and parameter names play no role in resolution.

title: Honoring a CancellationToken
question: An ASP.NET Core endpoint takes a CancellationToken and passes it to `db.Orders.ToListAsync(ct)`. The client disconnects mid-query. What happens?
options: The token is canceled, EF aborts the command and an OperationCanceledException propagates
Nothing; tokens only affect code that polls IsCancellationRequested manually
The query finishes and the response is buffered until the client reconnects
The server process is restarted to free the connection
explanation: ASP.NET Core binds a CancellationToken parameter to HttpContext.RequestAborted. Async APIs that accept the token observe it and stop work, throwing OperationCanceledException (or a TaskCanceledException subclass). Passing tokens through saves database and CPU time for abandoned requests.

title: Hierarchical keys in environment variables
question: Which environment variable overrides `Logging:LogLevel:Default` on Linux in an ASP.NET Core app?
options: Logging:LogLevel:Default (colon-separated)
Logging.LogLevel.Default (dot-separated)
Logging__LogLevel__Default (double underscores)
LOGGING_LOGLEVEL_DEFAULT (single underscores)
explanation: Colons are not allowed in environment variable names on all platforms, so the environment variables provider maps a double underscore to the ':' separator. Dots or single underscores are kept literally and don't create hierarchy. Keys are case-insensitive.

title: using declaration scope
options: Immediately after the WriteLine call
When the garbage collector finalizes the StreamWriter
At the end of the enclosing scope, after DoMoreWork returns
Never; using declarations only suppress warnings
explanation: A using declaration (C# 8+) disposes the variable when control leaves the enclosing block, here the method body, even if an exception is thrown. This is concise but can hold resources longer than a using block scoped tightly around the work.

title: Applying schema changes
question: After adding a property to an entity, which pair of EF Core CLI commands creates a migration and applies it to the database?
options: dotnet ef migrations add AddPhone, then dotnet ef database update
dotnet ef dbcontext scaffold, then dotnet ef database update
dotnet ef migrations add AddPhone, then dotnet build
dotnet ef database drop, then dotnet ef migrations list
explanation: migrations add compares the model to the last snapshot and generates Up/Down code; database update applies pending migrations. dbcontext scaffold reverse-engineers code from an existing database, and building alone never changes the schema.

title: Choosing a type for money
question: A C# billing service stores prices as double. Adding 0.10 ten times yields 0.9999999999999999 instead of 1.0, and invoices are off by a cent. Which type should hold the money amounts?
options: float, since its smaller size reduces the accumulated rounding error
decimal, since it represents base-10 fractions like 0.10 exactly
double, rounded with Math.Round after every addition to fix the drift
BigInteger, since only arbitrary precision removes rounding entirely
explanation: double is a binary floating-point type, so 0.10 has no exact representation and errors accumulate. decimal is a base-10 floating-point type with 28-29 significant digits, so amounts like 0.10 are exact, which is why it is recommended for financial values. float is even less precise, rounding after each step only hides the symptom, and BigInteger cannot hold fractions at all.

title: Unmatched C# switch expression
options: It throws a SwitchExpressionException because no arm matched
It returns null, because no arm matched the input value
It returns string.Empty, the default for string results
Nothing; the compiler rejects the non-exhaustive switch with an error
explanation: The compiler only emits warning CS8509 for a non-exhaustive switch expression, so the code builds. At runtime, when no pattern matches, .NET throws System.Runtime.CompilerServices.SwitchExpressionException rather than returning null or a default value. Add a discard arm (_ => ...) that returns a fallback or throws a meaningful exception.

title: Passing an int by value and by ref
explanation: By default C# passes arguments by value: AddTen receives a copy of n and changes only that copy, so n is still 5 afterwards. With ref, AddTenRef works on the caller's variable itself, so n becomes 15. 25 would need both calls to change n, and 5 would mean ref made no difference.

title: Culture-sensitive case conversion
question: A C# check uses ext.ToUpper() == "FILE". It passes in tests but fails on servers whose current culture is tr-TR. Why, and what is the fix?
options: Turkish upper-cases i to dotted I (U+0130); compare with OrdinalIgnoreCase
tr-TR stores strings as UTF-32 internally; convert both sides to UTF-8 first
ToUpper is evaluated lazily under some cultures; call ToString() to force it
tr-TR sorts capitals after lowercase; use String.Compare with CurrentCulture
explanation: ToUpper() uses the current culture, and in Turkish the lowercase dotted i maps to U+0130 (capital I with dot), so "file" becomes "FİLE" and the comparison fails. Identifiers, file extensions and protocol tokens should use string.Equals(a, b, StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase) or invariant casing. .NET strings are always UTF-16 and ToUpper is not lazy.

title: String concatenation in a loop
question: A C# report builder runs result += line; for 100,000 lines and is very slow. What is the main reason?
options: Strings are immutable, so each += copies everything: O(n^2) total
Strings are stored as linked lists, so += walks every character
+= takes a global lock on the string intern pool
The garbage collector runs a full collection after every concatenation
explanation: Each concatenation allocates a new string and copies all previous characters, so total work grows quadratically with the output length. StringBuilder appends into a growable buffer with amortized O(1) per character and produces the final string once. There is no per-concatenation lock or forced GC.

title: & versus && in C#
options: & has higher precedence than !=, so the comparison is grouped incorrectly
& converts the bools to integers and Count is evaluated first
& on bools evaluates both operands, so list.Count runs on a null list
The compiler reorders the operands of & to evaluate the cheaper one first
explanation: For bool operands, & is the non-short-circuiting logical AND: it always evaluates the right operand. && skips the right operand when the left is false, which is what protects the null check. Operator precedence is not the issue here because != binds tighter than &.
